claim: Angioblasts are initially specified in the lateral plate mesoderm and migrate between the somites towards the midline.
source: Angioblasts are initially specified in the lateral plate mesoderm and migrate between the somites towards the midline, where they coalesce and assemble the DA and the CV underneath the notochord (NC) (Figure 1A,B–F, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by direct statement in text and referenced figures showing angioblast migration patterns

claim: Angioblasts coalesce and assemble the dorsal aorta and cardinal vein underneath the notochord.
source: Angioblasts are initially specified in the lateral plate mesoderm and migrate between the somites towards the midline, where they coalesce and assemble the DA and the CV underneath the notochord (NC) (Figure 1A,B–F, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by direct statement in text and referenced figures and video showing vessel assembly

claim: VEGF-A has been proposed to serve as a chemoattractant for angioblasts and to regulate medial migration.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor has been proposed to serve as a chemoattractant for the angioblasts and to regulate this medial migration.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature proposing this mechanism

claim: Angioblasts rely on their intrinsic expression of Apelin receptors (Aplr, APJ) for their migration to the midline.
source: Here we challenge this model and instead demonstrate that angioblasts rely on their intrinsic expression of Apelin receptors (Aplr, APJ) for their migration to the midline.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including morpholino knockdown and mutant analysis

claim: During angioblast migration, Apelin receptor signaling is mainly triggered by the ligand Elabela (Ela).
source: We further show that during this angioblast migration Apelin receptor signaling is mainly triggered by the recently discovered ligand Elabela (Ela).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ela mutant phenotypes and expression patterns

claim: Neither Ela, Apelin, nor their receptors have previously been implicated in regulating angioblast migration.
source: As neither of the ligands Ela or Apelin (Apln) nor their receptors have previously been implicated in regulating angioblast migration, we hereby provide a novel mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis, with direct relevance to physiological and pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: Supported by lack of prior literature on this specific role

claim: The Ela-Aplnr signaling pathway represents a novel mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis.
source: As neither of the ligands Ela or Apelin (Apln) nor their receptors have previously been implicated in regulating angioblast migration, we hereby provide a novel mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis, with direct relevance to physiological and pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: vegfaa transcripts are present in the somites between 12 and 15 hours post fertilization.
source: As previously published (Nicoli et al., 2008), expression analysis of vegfaa, the gene for the main VEGF-A ortholog in zebrafish, showed the presence of transcripts in the somites between 12 and 15 hr post fertilization (hpf), that is the stage when angioblasts migrate to the midline (see Figure 1B–F).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and referenced figures

claim: Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) does not interfere with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos.
source: Surprisingly, neither Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) nor a null mutation in the gene encoding the VEGFR2 ortholog (kdrl) interfered with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos (Figure 1H,J), although Vegfa signaling dependent phenotypes, like failure to form the intersegmental vessels, could be observed after 24 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in figures

claim: A null mutation in the kdrl gene (encoding VEGFR2 ortholog) does not interfere with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos.
source: Surprisingly, neither Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) nor a null mutation in the gene encoding the VEGFR2 ortholog (kdrl) interfered with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos (Figure 1H,J), although Vegfa signaling dependent phenotypes, like failure to form the intersegmental vessels, could be observed after 24 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genetic mutant analysis shown in figures

claim: Vegfa signaling deficiency causes failure to form intersegmental vessels after 24 hpf.
source: Surprisingly, neither Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) nor a null mutation in the gene encoding the VEGFR2 ortholog (kdrl) interfered with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos (Figure 1H,J), although Vegfa signaling dependent phenotypes, like failure to form the intersegmental vessels, could be observed after 24 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing later vascular defects in Vegfa-deficient embryos

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Vegfr2 signaling from 6 to 17 hpf does not impair angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Additionally, pharmacological inhibition of Vegfr2 signaling from 6 to 17 hpf did not impair angioblast migration to the midline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemical inhibitor treatment shown in supplementary figure

claim: Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) activity in the midline induces vegfaa expression.
source: As activity of Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) in the midline has been shown to induce vegfaa expression (Lawson et al., 2002), we repeated the published experiments and blocked this process by chemical inhibition of Shh signaling using cyclopamine.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: Angioblast migration is not affected after Shh inhibition.
source: In line with our previous experiments, angioblast migration was not affected after Shh inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cyclopamine treatment shown in supplementary figure

claim: Vegfa signaling is dispensable for angioblast specification or migration in zebrafish.
source: The sum of these data strongly indicates that Vegfa signaling is dispensable for angioblast specification or migration in zebrafish.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches showing no effect of Vegfa loss on angioblast migration

claim: Apelin is expressed by the notochord.
source: As previously published (Zeng et al., 2007), we detected the expression of Apelin, a short secreted peptide encoded by the apln gene, by the NC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure and cited prior work

claim: Transcripts of apelin receptor a (aplnra) and apelin receptor b (aplnrb) are present in angioblasts.
source: At the same time, transcripts of its two paralogous receptors apelin receptor a (aplnra) and apelin receptor b (aplnrb) were present in angioblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B; [Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007]).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure and cited prior work

claim: Both aplnra and aplnrb are important for midline migration of angioblasts.
source: Using MO-mediated gene knockdown, we observed that both aplnra and aplnrb are important for midline migration of angioblasts.
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown experiments showing migration defects

claim: Absence of each individual apelin receptor reduces the efficiency of angioblast migration towards the midline.
source: While absence of each individual receptor reduced the efficiency of migration towards the midline, double depletion completely abolished this process (Figure 2A, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in figure and video

claim: Double depletion of aplnra and aplnrb completely abolishes angioblast migration to the midline.
source: While absence of each individual receptor reduced the efficiency of migration towards the midline, double depletion completely abolished this process (Figure 2A, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in figure and video

claim: Homozygous aplnr mutant embryos phenocopy the MO-induced phenotypes.
source: Homozygous mutant embryos phenocopied the MO-induced phenotypes, additional loss of one or two copies of the second receptor increased the severity of the phenotype (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by genetic mutant analysis shown in figure

claim: Additional loss of one or two copies of the second apelin receptor increases the severity of the angioblast migration phenotype.
source: Homozygous mutant embryos phenocopied the MO-induced phenotypes, additional loss of one or two copies of the second receptor increased the severity of the phenotype (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis of double heterozygous crosses shown in figure

claim: aplnrb transcripts are detected together with the angioblast specification marker etv2.
source: Additionally, we detected aplnrb transcripts together with the angioblast specification marker etv2 indicating that both genes are expressed very early during angioblast specification.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing co-expression

claim: Apln receptors only regulate angioblast migration, but not specification.
source: However, when we analyzed aplnra/aplnrb double deficient embryos, no difference in etv2 expression was detectable by in situ hybridization indicating that Apln receptors only regulate angioblast migration, but not specification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing normal etv2 expression in receptor-deficient embryos

claim: MO-mediated knockdown of apln does not affect angioblast migration.
source: Next, we analyzed the requirement for the ligand Apln by MO-mediated gene knockdown and, unexpectedly, observed no difference to control MO injected embryos (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in figure

claim: Homozygous aplnmu267 mutant embryos show no vasculogenesis defects.
source: Consistent with the MO-mediated depletion, homozygous aplnmu267 mutant embryos (Figure 2A) showed no vasculogenesis defects, which indicated that endogenous Apln is not sufficient to regulate angioblast migration to the midline.
evidence: Supported by genetic mutant analysis shown in figure

claim: Endogenous Apln is not sufficient to regulate angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Consistent with the MO-mediated depletion, homozygous aplnmu267 mutant embryos (Figure 2A) showed no vasculogenesis defects, which indicated that endogenous Apln is not sufficient to regulate angioblast migration to the midline.
evidence: Supported by lack of phenotype in apln mutants despite receptor requirement

claim: Apelin receptors are required for myocardial development in zebrafish.
source: Previous studies have identified a requirement for Apln receptors in myocardial development in zebrafish (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007) and mice (Charo et al., 2009), which could not completely be phenocopied by Apln deficiency (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007; Charo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Apelin receptors are required for myocardial development in mice.
source: Previous studies have identified a requirement for Apln receptors in myocardial development in zebrafish (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007) and mice (Charo et al., 2009), which could not completely be phenocopied by Apln deficiency (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007; Charo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Apln deficiency could not completely phenocopy Apln receptor deficiency in myocardial development.
source: Previous studies have identified a requirement for Apln receptors in myocardial development in zebrafish (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007) and mice (Charo et al., 2009), which could not completely be phenocopied by Apln deficiency (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007; Charo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Elabela (Ela) is a novel peptide hormone that binds and activates Apelin receptors.
source: Recently, a novel peptide hormone named Elabela (Ela, also known as Apela or Toddler) was identified in zebrafish and shown to bind and activate Aplnrs (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent publications identifying Ela

claim: ela is expressed by the notochord.
source: By in situ hybridization we detected ela expression by the NC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, [Pauli et al., 2014]), consistent with a possible role in attracting angioblasts to the midline.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure and cited work

claim: Ela deficiency leads to a strong impairment of angioblast migration.
source: We next analyzed angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos carrying a homozygous null mutation in the ela gene (elabr13). Ela deficiency led to a strong impairment of angioblast migration (Figure 2A), indicating that indeed Ela-Aplnr represent a novel bona fide ligand–receptor pair and therefore a novel signaling pathway regulating angioblast migration.
evidence: Supported by genetic mutant analysis shown in figure

claim: Ela-Aplnr represent a novel bona fide ligand-receptor pair regulating angioblast migration.
source: We next analyzed angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos carrying a homozygous null mutation in the ela gene (elabr13). Ela deficiency led to a strong impairment of angioblast migration (Figure 2A), indicating that indeed Ela-Aplnr represent a novel bona fide ligand–receptor pair and therefore a novel signaling pathway regulating angioblast migration.
evidence: Supported by genetic and expression data showing ligand-receptor relationship

claim: apln expression increases later in the notochord while ela expression becomes progressively reduced.
source: Given that the ela-/- phenotype was not as severe as the depletion of both receptors and that apln expression increases later in the NC (while ela expression becomes progressively reduced, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), we analyzed the phenotypes of the offspring of apln+/−;ela+/− double heterozygous parents.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data at different time points shown in supplementary figure

claim: A mild angioblast migration phenotype is observed when either one ela or both apln alleles are mutant.
source: Interestingly a mild phenotype was observed, when either one ela or both apln alleles were mutant, a strong phenotype when ela was homozygously mutant with increasing severity (severe phenotype) upon loss of the apln alleles (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis of double heterozygous crosses shown in figure

claim: A strong angioblast migration phenotype is observed when ela is homozygously mutant.
source: Interestingly a mild phenotype was observed, when either one ela or both apln alleles were mutant, a strong phenotype when ela was homozygously mutant with increasing severity (severe phenotype) upon loss of the apln alleles (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis of double heterozygous crosses shown in figure

claim: Phenotypic severity increases upon loss of apln alleles in ela mutant embryos.
source: Interestingly a mild phenotype was observed, when either one ela or both apln alleles were mutant, a strong phenotype when ela was homozygously mutant with increasing severity (severe phenotype) upon loss of the apln alleles (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis showing dose-dependent effects

claim: Homozygous ela−/−; apln−/− double mutants phenocopy apln receptor deficiency.
source: Homozygous ela−/−; apln−/− double mutants phenocopied apln receptor deficiency (compare in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis comparing double ligand mutants to receptor mutants

claim: Ela acts as the major endogenous attractant for angioblast migration to the midline.
source: The observed dose dependency is indicative, that in this context Ela and Apln might act as novel chemoattractants for angioblast migration to the midline, with Ela acting as the major endogenous attractant and Apln having a minor additive role.
evidence: Supported by genetic dose-dependency analysis showing stronger ela phenotype

claim: Apln has a minor additive role in angioblast migration to the midline.
source: The observed dose dependency is indicative, that in this context Ela and Apln might act as novel chemoattractants for angioblast migration to the midline, with Ela acting as the major endogenous attractant and Apln having a minor additive role.
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis showing mild phenotype only when ela is also mutant

claim: Signals from the midline guide angioblast migration.
source: Previous analysis of zebrafish embryos lacking the NC showed, that signals from the midline guide angioblast migration (Fouquet et al., 1997; Sumoy et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Angioblast migration is perturbed in notochord homeobox (noto) mutants lacking a notochord.
source: We could show that indeed angioblast migration as well as ela expression is perturbed in the zebrafish mutants lacking a NC (notochord homeobox, noto; previous name: floating head) or exhibiting defective NC precursor differentiation (T, brachyury homolog a, ta; previous name: no tail) (Figure 3) (Halpern et al., 1993; Odenthal et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genetic mutants shown in figure

claim: Angioblast migration is perturbed in brachyury homolog a (ta) mutants exhibiting defective notochord precursor differentiation.
source: We could show that indeed angioblast migration as well as ela expression is perturbed in the zebrafish mutants lacking a NC (notochord homeobox, noto; previous name: floating head) or exhibiting defective NC precursor differentiation (T, brachyury homolog a, ta; previous name: no tail) (Figure 3) (Halpern et al., 1993; Odenthal et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genetic mutants shown in figure

claim: ela expression is perturbed in noto mutants.
source: We could show that indeed angioblast migration as well as ela expression is perturbed in the zebrafish mutants lacking a NC (notochord homeobox, noto; previous name: floating head) or exhibiting defective NC precursor differentiation (T, brachyury homolog a, ta; previous name: no tail) (Figure 3) (Halpern et al., 1993; Odenthal et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in mutants shown in figure

claim: ela expression is perturbed in ta mutants.
source: We could show that indeed angioblast migration as well as ela expression is perturbed in the zebrafish mutants lacking a NC (notochord homeobox, noto; previous name: floating head) or exhibiting defective NC precursor differentiation (T, brachyury homolog a, ta; previous name: no tail) (Figure 3) (Halpern et al., 1993; Odenthal et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in mutants shown in figure

claim: Angioblasts in nototk241 mutant embryos fail to migrate to the midline.
source: While angioblasts in nototk241 mutant embryos failed to migrate to the midline, tab160 angioblasts migrated towards the midline but failed to reach this structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in figure

claim: tab160 angioblasts migrate towards the midline but fail to reach this structure.
source: While angioblasts in nototk241 mutant embryos failed to migrate to the midline, tab160 angioblasts migrated towards the midline but failed to reach this structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in figure

claim: ela expression is strongly diminished in the tab160 midline.
source: In line with these results, ela expression was strongly diminished in the tab160 midline and almost absent in nototk241 mutant embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figure

claim: ela expression is almost absent in nototk241 mutant embryos.
source: In line with these results, ela expression was strongly diminished in the tab160 midline and almost absent in nototk241 mutant embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figure

claim: Ela overexpression in the midline restores angioblast migration in tab160 embryos.
source: Indeed, Ela overexpression did restore angioblast migration to the midline in tab160 embryos (Figure 3C), demonstrating that midline Ela expression is not only necessary, but sufficient to regulate angioblast migration during vasculogenesis.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments using shh promoter-driven ela expression shown in figure

claim: Midline Ela expression is necessary and sufficient to regulate angioblast migration during vasculogenesis.
source: Indeed, Ela overexpression did restore angioblast migration to the midline in tab160 embryos (Figure 3C), demonstrating that midline Ela expression is not only necessary, but sufficient to regulate angioblast migration during vasculogenesis.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function and rescue experiments

claim: Ela does not act as a chemoattractant but instead acts as a motogen in regulating mesoderm migration during gastrulation.
source: Recently, it was published that Ela does not act as a chemoattractant, but instead acts as a motogen in regulating mesoderm migration during gastrulation (Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: aplnr deficient angioblasts are still partially motile and send out filopodia, but fail to migrate to the midline.
source: In contrast, the aplnr deficient (aplra/b MO injected) angioblasts were still partially motile and did send out filopodia, but failed to migrate to the midline (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse video analysis of morpholino-injected embryos

claim: More than 52% of angioblasts are close to Ela overexpressing cells in noto or ta mutant embryos.
source: While only 20% of the angioblast were found in the vicinity of control cells, more than 52% of the angioblasts were close to Ela overexpressing cells (Figure 4D,G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ectopic Ela expression experiments shown in figure

claim: Only 20% of angioblasts are found in the vicinity of control cells in noto or ta mutant embryos.
source: While only 20% of the angioblast were found in the vicinity of control cells, more than 52% of the angioblasts were close to Ela overexpressing cells (Figure 4D,G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of control experiments shown in figure

claim: Ela acts as a chemoattractant for angioblasts during midline migration.
source: Together with the observed dose dependency of Ela-Apln, the motility of Aplnr deficient embryos and the rescue of NC mutants by midline Ela expression, our data support the interpretation, that Ela acts as a chemoattractant for angioblasts during midline migration.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including dose dependency, motility analysis, and ectopic expression

claim: 93.6% of control MO-injected transplanted angioblasts migrate to the midline in a WT host embryo.
source: Analysis of angioblast migration to the midline at 17 hpf revealed that in average 93.6% of control MO-injected transplanted angioblasts migrated to the midline in a WT host embryo (Figure 5B,C; n = 39 GFP+ angioblasts, 7 embryos).
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in figure

claim: Only 9.4% of aplnra/b MO injected angioblasts arrive at the midline in WT host embryos.
source: In contrast, only 9.4% of aplnra/b MO injected angioblasts arrived at the midline, whereas the majority of these cells remained in more lateral positions (Figure 5B,D; n = 62 GFP+ angioblasts, 5 embryos).
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in figure

claim: 81.9% of transplanted WT angioblasts migrate to the midline in an aplnr deficient environment.
source: Transplanted WT angioblasts were perfectly capable to migrate to the midline in an aplnr deficient environment (average of 81.9%, Figure 5B,E; n = 15 GFP+ angioblasts, 6 embryos), which shows that there is indeed a cell autonomous requirement for Aplnr signaling in angioblasts.
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in figure

claim: There is a cell autonomous requirement for Aplnr signaling in angioblasts.
source: Transplanted WT angioblasts were perfectly capable to migrate to the midline in an aplnr deficient environment (average of 81.9%, Figure 5B,E; n = 15 GFP+ angioblasts, 6 embryos), which shows that there is indeed a cell autonomous requirement for Aplnr signaling in angioblasts.
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments showing receptor requirement in donor cells

claim: Ela expression at the embryonic midline provides a chemoattractive signal for Aplnr-positive angioblasts.
source: Based on the sum of the results presented above, we propose that Ela expression at the embryonic midline provides a chemoattractive signal for Aplnr-positive angioblasts.
evidence: Supported by the sum of experimental evidence including expression, loss-of-function, and ectopic expression studies

claim: The initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln.
source: While Ela and Apln both signal to the Apln receptors, the initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln, which peaked at later developmental time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data at different time points shown in supplementary figure

claim: apln expression peaks at later developmental time points than ela.
source: While Ela and Apln both signal to the Apln receptors, the initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln, which peaked at later developmental time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data at different time points shown in supplementary figure

claim: ela and apln may have partially redundant functions, but are required at different stages of vascular morphogenesis.
source: Thus, ela and apln may have partially redundant functions, but are required at different stages of vascular morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by temporal expression differences and genetic interaction data

claim: Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts.
source: Surprisingly, while Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts, this process was not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function experiments showing complete block of migration

claim: Angioblast migration is not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
source: Surprisingly, while Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts, this process was not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function experiments showing no effect on migration

claim: Ela-Aplnr signaling represents a novel signaling pathway for angioblasts regulating vascular patterning in the developing vertebrate embryo.
source: Our studies identified Ela-Aplnr signaling as a novel signaling pathway for angioblasts regulating vascular patterning in the developing vertebrate embryo.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive experimental characterization of this pathway

claim: The Ela-Aplnr signaling pathway may represent a novel therapeutic target in human disease.
source: As therapeutic intervention with vascular growth is clinically highly relevant and, so far, predominantly focuses on the VEGF-A signaling cascade, the Ela-Aplnr signaling pathway may also represent a novel therapeutic target in human disease.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the discovery of a novel vascular signaling pathway

claim: Global inactivation of VEGF-A in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the dorsal aorta.
source: Global inactivation of the genes encoding VEGF-A or the corresponding receptor VEGFR2 in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the DA (Shalaby et al., 1995; Ferrara et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work in mice

claim: Global inactivation of VEGFR2 in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the dorsal aorta.
source: Global inactivation of the genes encoding VEGF-A or the corresponding receptor VEGFR2 in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the DA (Shalaby et al., 1995; Ferrara et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work in mice

claim: In Xenopus embryos, vegfa transcripts are expressed in the midline.
source: In Xenopus embryos, transcripts for the vegfa gene are expressed in the midline and migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression (Cleaver and Krieg, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work in Xenopus

claim: In Xenopus embryos, migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression.
source: In Xenopus embryos, transcripts for the vegfa gene are expressed in the midline and migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression (Cleaver and Krieg, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work in Xenopus

claim: vegfaa is the gene for the main VEGF-A ortholog in zebrafish.
source: As previously published (Nicoli et al., 2008), expression analysis of vegfaa, the gene for the main VEGF-A ortholog in zebrafish, showed the presence of transcripts in the somites between 12 and 15 hr post fertilization (hpf), that is the stage when angioblasts migrate to the midline (see Figure 1B–F).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge of zebrafish orthologs

claim: Angioblasts migrate to the midline between 12 and 15 hours post fertilization.
source: As previously published (Nicoli et al., 2008), expression analysis of vegfaa, the gene for the main VEGF-A ortholog in zebrafish, showed the presence of transcripts in the somites between 12 and 15 hr post fertilization (hpf), that is the stage when angioblasts migrate to the midline (see Figure 1B–F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and staging information

claim: Embryos were staged by counting somites, with 16-17 somites equivalent to 17 hpf.
source: To rule out developmental delays, we counted the somites of the embryos and fixed them for confocal analysis, when they had developed 16–17 somites (equivalent to 17 hpf).
evidence: Supported by standard zebrafish staging methods

claim: Elabela is also known as Apela or Toddler.
source: Recently, a novel peptide hormone named Elabela (Ela, also known as Apela or Toddler) was identified in zebrafish and shown to bind and activate Aplnrs (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications using different names for the same peptide

claim: TALEN or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to introduce mutations in aplnra, aplnrb, and apln genes.
source: We used TALEN or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing (Hwang et al., 2013; Jao et al., 2013) to introduce mutations in either the aplnra or the aplnrb gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by methods description and supplementary figure showing mutations

claim: The aplnramu296 mutation is an 8 base pair insertion leading to a premature stop and shortening of the Aplnra protein to 13 amino acids.
source: An 8 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnra protein to 13 AA.
evidence: Supported by sequence data shown in supplementary figure

claim: The aplnrbmu270 mutation is a 4 base pair insertion leading to a premature stop and shortening of the Aplnrb protein to 65 amino acids.
source: A 4 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnrb protein to 65 AA.
evidence: Supported by sequence data shown in supplementary figure

claim: The aplnmu267 mutation is a 1 base pair loss / 9 base pair insertion causing a frameshift leading to a premature stop codon and shortening of the Apln protein to 11 amino acids.
source: An 1 baise pair loss / 9 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue causes a frameshift leading to a premature stop codon and a shortening of the Apln protein to 11 AA.
evidence: Supported by sequence data shown in supplementary figure

claim: aplnra is expressed in the paraxial mesoderm at 12 hpf.
source: At 12 hpf, aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts (prior to migration, arrowheads) and within the lateral plate mesoderm and at the notochord somite boundary. aplnra expression is strong in the paraxial mesoderm (A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts prior to migration at 12 hpf.
source: At 12 hpf, aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts (prior to migration, arrowheads) and within the lateral plate mesoderm and at the notochord somite boundary.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: aplnrb is expressed within the lateral plate mesoderm and at the notochord somite boundary at 12 hpf.
source: At 12 hpf, aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts (prior to migration, arrowheads) and within the lateral plate mesoderm and at the notochord somite boundary.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Both aplnra and aplnrb are expressed in the angioblasts at 18 hpf.
source: Both receptors are expressed in the angioblasts at 18 hpf (A, B, arrowheads) and in the developing axial vessels at 20 hpf (Arrowheads point to the DA, arrows to the PCV).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Both aplnra and aplnrb are expressed in the developing axial vessels at 20 hpf.
source: Both receptors are expressed in the angioblasts at 18 hpf (A, B, arrowheads) and in the developing axial vessels at 20 hpf (Arrowheads point to the DA, arrows to the PCV).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Prior to angioblast migration, apln and ela are both expressed by the notochord, with ela showing much stronger expression.
source: Prior to angioblast migration apln and ela are both expressed by the notochord, with ela showing a much stronger expression (C, D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figure

claim: After angioblasts reach the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf), only apln is still expressed by the notochord, whereas notochord-derived ela expression is strongly reduced to absent.
source: After angioblasts reached the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf) only apln is still expressed by the notochord, whereas notochord derived ela expression is strongly reduced to absent.
